name: bloaty
why: Shows where every byte in a binary goes, a useful lens for taking compiled programs apart.

brief.what_it_is: Bloaty is a command-line size profiler for compiled binaries. You point it at an ELF, Mach-O, PE/COFF, or WebAssembly file (or an object file or static library), and it prints a table that breaks the file down by sections, symbols, segments, compile units, inlines, or input files, showing how many bytes each piece takes on disk (FILE SIZE) and in memory (VM SIZE). It can also compare two binaries and show which parts grew or shrank. Output is human-readable by default, with --csv and --tsv options.
brief.why_it_exists: The README asks 'Ever wondered what's making your binary big?' and says Bloaty will show a size profile so you can understand what is taking up space inside a binary. It says it aims to attribute every byte of the binary to the symbol or compile unit that produced it.
brief.how_it_works: Bloaty uses its own ELF, DWARF, and Mach-O parsers rather than relying on external tools. It maps each byte of the file to a section, segment, symbol, or debug-info entry, and it will disassemble the binary to find references to anonymous data. Debug-based sources such as compileunits and symbols need debug information, which can live in a separate file matched by build ID.

brief.install_notes: The README says to build with CMake (configure, build, optional install), with Ninja as one example generator. Bloaty bundles libprotobuf, re2, capstone, and pkg-config as Git submodules and prefers system copies if present. If the repo was not cloned recursively, run git submodule update --init --recursive. Tests are described in tests/README.md. The brew formula gave no caveats. Separate debug files need build IDs: gcc adds them by default, while Clang needs -Wl,--build-id on the link line.
brief.standout: Bloaty is a statically linked C++ binary built on its own parsers, and it attributes bytes by source compile unit and by inlined source line, not just by symbol. Its size-diff mode is pitched for CI, and custom data sources are RE2 regex rewrites of built-in breakdowns, so you can bucket results by library or package.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a GitHub Actions build badge and says 'GitHub issues and PRs welcome', but I saw no release date, version number, or last-commit date in the pages I read, so I cannot say whether it is active.
brief.caveats: PE/COFF and WebAssembly support are marked experimental, and --disassemble is marked EXPERIMENTAL. Separate debug files depend on build IDs; the README says GNU debuglink and build-ID lookup of debug files are not supported. Clang does not add build IDs by default, so you may need to add -Wl,--build-id. Some data sources do not work on object files, especially those that read debug info. Building needs CMake and submodules. The README says: This is not an official Google product. The license was not checked in the pages I read.

easy to deploy: statically-linked C++ binary, easy to copy around

entry.title: Bloaty
entry.tldr: Bloaty breaks a compiled binary down by section, symbol, or source file, showing where every byte went and what grew between builds.
entry.deeper_look:
Bloaty is a command-line size profiler. You give it a compiled file (ELF, Mach-O, and experimentally PE/COFF or WebAssembly, plus object files and static libraries) and it prints a table of how many bytes each piece takes on disk (FILE SIZE) and in memory (VM SIZE). You choose the breakdown: sections, segments, symbols, compile units, inlines, or input files.

The README opens with a question: "Ever wondered what's making your binary big?" It aims to attribute every byte of the binary to the symbol or compile unit that produced it. To do that it uses its own ELF, DWARF, and Mach-O parsers instead of calling external tools. It maps each byte to a section, segment, symbol, or debug-info entry, and it can disassemble the binary to find references to anonymous data.

The idea underneath is that a binary is a map you can read. Breakdowns can be stacked, so you can see segments, then sections within them, then symbols within those. A diff mode compares two binaries and shows which parts grew or shrank, which is how it gets pitched for CI. Custom data sources are regex rewrites of the built-in breakdowns, so you can bucket results by library or package.

Debug-based views such as compileunits and symbols need debug info. That info can live in a separate file matched by build ID, which lets you profile a stripped binary.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the full option list, including --demangle, -n, -s, --domain, and --source-filter.
Prints a hierarchical profile, with sections nested under segments, for the binary you name.
Shows a size diff: the file after -- is the base, and the table shows what grew or shrank.

entry.whats_unique: It attributes bytes to source compile units and inlined source lines, not just symbols, using its own parsers. Its diff mode and regex-based custom data sources suit tracking size in CI.
entry.caveats: PE/COFF, WebAssembly, and --disassemble are marked experimental, separate debug files need build IDs (Clang needs -Wl,--build-id), and the README says it is not an official Google product.
